newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian minister quits in fodder scandal.
newsitem.headline: Indian minister quits in fodder scandal.

text.p: An Indian minister resigned on Friday as shock waves from a $280-million corruption scandal spread to Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's two-month-old government.
Junior Rural Areas and Employment Minister Chandradeo Prasad Varma said he was innocent in the fodder scandal but had decided to bow to Gujral, who earlier on Friday had asked him to step down.

"I am not involved in the scam but abide by the directive of the prime minister," Varma told Reuters in the capital of eastern Bihar state, Patna. "I have faxed my resignation letter to the prime minister."
Varma spoke after meeting Bihar chief minister Laloo Prasad Yadav, who with Varma is among 56 people accused in the case.
"I have faith in the judiciary and will fight the case in court," the Press Trust of India quoted Varma as saying.
On Tuesday, the Bihar governor authorised federal police to prosecute Varma and Yadav in the corruption scandal.
The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) was expected to indict Varma, Yadav and 54 others in the case later on Friday or Saturday, officials told Reuters.
Yadav, who is president of Gujral's Janata Dal party, has said he is innocent in the scandal, which dates back to the 1980s and involves the alleged siphoning off of animal welfare funds.

The CBI had sought permission from the state governor to pursue legal proceedings against Yadav and Varma. The charges against Yadav will carry a maximum penalty of seven years in jail, CBI officials said.
Both Yadav and Varma have asked a local court for preventive bail to stop them being arrested in the case.

The scandal has stoked tension in the Janata Dal, which is the biggest group in Gujral's 15-party United Front coalition, and has presented the prime minister with his biggest political challenge since he took office in late April.
Leftwing parties in Gujral's centre-left alliance have been pressing for Yadav and Varma to step down.

"Morally and ethically, they can't continue and so they have to vacate their offices," Atul Anjan, national secretary of the Communist Party of India, part of the United Front, told Reuters. "Mr Laloo Yadav should read the writing on the wall."
Yadav is locked in a party election tussle with challenger Sharad Yadav, who is no relation but a key rival in the low-caste Yadav community to which they both belong.
Mutual mistrust over party electoral proceedings has spilled over to courtrooms.
On Thursday, the Supreme Court appointed two senior Janata Dal leaders, Madhu Dandavate and Information and Broadcasting Minister Jaipal Reddy, to hold party elections by July 3.
